POLICING THE BARGAINING PROCESS 
Yielding to Threat 
How resistant must the pressured party be? And in the face of what 
degree of impermissible behavior? Is threatening 
extended civil litigation 
insufficiently severe? In Denbow v. Tesch, 278 N.W. 16 (S.D. 1938), a 
brother threatened 
his sister that unless 
she signed an agreement 
dividing their parents' estate, he would "law and law it" in court and she 
would get nothing. The sister signed and later sought to have the 
agreement cancelled. In upholding the agreement, the court stated: 
"Suffice it to say that if it be assumed that this feeble threat was effective 
in coercing the f' gnature 
of the plaintiff, it is not such a threat as will 
support a conclusion that the consent of the plaintiff was procured 
through duresR and menace." Do you agree? 
And wha degree of fortitude is required if the threat or pressure is 
more substantial? The homeowner in Wathins & Son seemed to cave 
quickly. Did} e meet the tandard of <lures and resistance suggested by 
one court of' ri:>$traint or danger, either actually inflicted or impending, 
which is suffi ient in severity or apprehension to overcome the mind of a 
person of ordinary firrnnes "? Carrier v. William Penn Broadcasting Co., 
233 A.2d 519 (Pa. 1967). Other court imply even stricter tests: duress, 
as they descrihe it, must d prive a person of free exercise of will, see 
Raymundo v .• ammond 
Clinic As 'n, 449 N.E.2d 276 (Ind. 1983), or 
destroy a person's volition, se Konsuvo v. Netzke, 220 A.2d 424 (N.J. 
1966). Such expressions, oft n somewhat metaphorical, appear largely in 
cases where relief was granted, and often in cases where no such total 
mastery over the innocent party xisted. 
A classic, 1 passage 
rejecting the "no will" conception of duress is 
from HolmeR· "It always is for the interest 
of a party under duress to 
choose the lec:;ser of two evils. But the fact that a choice was made 
according to interest does not exclude duress. It is the characteristic 
of 
duress properly so called." Union Pacific R. Co. v. Public Service Comm., 
248 U.S. 67 1 l918) (duress by a state agency). On the other hand, it is 
regularly acknowledged that a perfectly honorable agreement may be 
made with a person who must either accede to it or face some repugnant 
alternative. Tidwell v. 
ritz, 282 S.E.2d 104 (Ga. 1981). "The question is 
one of degree." Hellenic Lines, Ltd. v. Louis Dreyfus Corp., 372 F.2d 753 
(2d Cir. 1967).
